Plant Description: Fast-growing evergreen tree reaching up to 15-20 meters with wide-spreading branches.
Morphological Features: Leaves pinnate, leaflets lanceolate with serrate margins; white fragrant flowers; olive-like drupe fruit.
Distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent; widely planted across tropical and subtropical regions.
Habitat: Dry tropical and subtropical forests, open plains, and cultivated areas.
Uses: Extensively used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine, natural biopesticides, cosmetics, timber, and dental hygiene.

Plant Description: Medium to large evergreen tree capable of reaching 20 meters, known for producing massive cauliflorous fruit.
Morphological Features: Dense foliage with dark green, elliptical, leathery leaves; fruits huge, covered in hard conical tubercles.
Distribution: Native to Western Ghats and tropical Asia; widely cultivated across South and Southeast Asia.
Habitat: Tropical moist lowlands and intermediate zones with humid conditions.
Uses: Nutritious staple food source (flesh and seeds), high-quality timber for furniture and musical instruments, fodder.

Plant Description: Large semi-evergreen or deciduous banyan tree of great religious and cultural significance.
Morphological Features: Distinctive heart-shaped leaves with an elongated, slender drip tip; small paired figs turning purple when ripe.
Distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent and Indochina; widely cultivated throughout Asia.
Habitat: Found in both dry and moist forests, rocky outcrops, temple grounds, and urban landscapes.
Uses: Revered religious tree; bark, leaves, and latex used in Ayurveda for respiratory, digestive, and skin ailments.

Plant Description: Large evergreen tree reaching 30-40 meters with a broad, rounded spreading canopy.
Morphological Features: Leaves alternate, simple, oblong-lanceolate; branched panicles of small fragrant flowers; fleshy oval/kidney drupes.
Distribution: Native to South and Southeast Asia; naturalized globally in tropical and warm subtropical areas.
Habitat: Lowland tropical forests, riverine valleys, orchards, and home gardens.
Uses: Prized edible fruit eaten ripe or unripe, juice, pickles; wood for light timber; medicinal uses in local therapies.

Plant Description: Long-lived, slow-growing, medium-to-large evergreen tree up to 25 meters tall with graceful feathery foliage.
Morphological Features: Pinnately compound leaves with 10-20 pairs of leaflets; pale yellow flowers with red streaks; pod fruits with tart pulp.
Distribution: Indigenous to tropical Africa; widely naturalized and cultivated across South Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Americas.
Habitat: Dry zones, semi-arid savannahs, road verges, and agroforestry systems.
Uses: Pulp used as souring culinary agent, chutneys, beverages; hard timber for carving; medicinal digestive aid.

Plant Description: Small to medium-sized hemiparasitic evergreen tree up to 10-15 meters tall.
Morphological Features: Opposite, thin, glabrous elliptic leaves; small purplish-red flowers; globose fleshy drupes.
Distribution: Native to Southern India, Sri Lanka, and parts of Indonesia and Australasia.
Habitat: Dry deciduous scrub forests, open woodlands, well-drained soils.
Uses: Valuable aromatic essential oil extracted from heartwood; incense, perfumery, sacred rituals, fine carving, skin treatments.

Plant Description: Fast-growing tropical evergreen tree reaching 20-30 meters with a dense foliage crown.
Morphological Features: Opposite, leathery, elliptic-oblong leaves with subtle turpentine aroma; small white flowers; dark purple oblong berries.
Distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia; naturalized widely in the tropics.
Habitat: Moist riverbanks, wet lowlands, secondary forests, and cultivated lands.
Uses: Edible astringent sweet fruits; seed extracts traditionally used to regulate blood sugar in diabetes; durable timber.

Scientific Name: Terminalia arjuna (Roxb. ex DC.) Wight & Arn.
Plant Description: Majestic riverine evergreen tree growing up to 25 meters with extensive buttress roots and smooth greenish-white bark.
Morphological Features: Smooth peeling bark; oblong sub-opposite leaves; small yellowish-white flowers; five-winged fibrous woody fruit.
Distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent, prominently found along river systems in Sri Lanka and India.
Habitat: Riverbanks, stream margins, alluvial flood plains, and wet lowland forest peripheries.
Uses: Famous in Ayurvedic cardiology (cardioprotective bark tonics); riverbank erosion control; shade tree; construction wood.

Plant Description: Herbaceous perennial growing annual pseudostems about 1 meter tall from an underground aromatic rhizome.
Morphological Features: Narrow linear-lanceolate leaves; cone-like spikes of pale yellow and purple flowers; thick, pungent, branched rhizomes.
Distribution: Native to Maritime Southeast Asia; cultivated globally across tropical and subtropical regions.
Habitat: Humid tropical lowlands and mid-elevations under partial shade or open cultivation.
Uses: World-renowned culinary spice, herbal teas, confectionery; remedy for nausea, digestion, inflammation, and cold symptoms.

Plant Description: Perennial climbing woody vine that grows up to 4-10 meters using adventitious aerial rootlets.
Morphological Features: Altering ovate leathery leaves; pendulous flower spikes bearing 50-60 small flowers; drupes maturing from green to red.
Distribution: Native to the Western Ghats of South India; widely cultivated in Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, and Brazil.
Habitat: Moist, warm tropical rainforests and shaded agroforestry plantations.
Uses: The 'King of Spices' (black, white, and green peppercorns); digestive stimulant, food seasoning, preservative, and Ayurvedic medicine.
